title: A short poem came my way. It says something really important about learning.
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton reads a brief poem, Brackets by Chitra Kalyani, in which a French teacher puts pupils' errors in brackets with a polite suggestion rather than crossing them out. Through his learning lens he draws three lessons. Mistakes are the evidence of how learning begins, not of failure. Keeping them visible is a form of kindness and also what it means to be genuinely learning-focused. The third lesson corrects his own long-held slogan: the word yet is only credible once a learner has already seen their own improvement, so an early yet is an empty promise. He concludes that teachers should preserve and revisit mistakes so that students can later be told they made them and no longer do.
points: Mistakes mark where learning starts and should be treated as evidence of progress rather than something to hide or airbrush away.
Leaving errors visible alongside a suggestion for improvement is both a kind act and a learning-focused one.
Telling a struggling student they cannot do it yet carries little weight until they have seen their own earlier mistakes turn into competence.
Recalling a past mistake and showing it has been overcome gives students personal, evidenced proof that they can become better learners.
quotes: Through that lens, the first thing I love about this poem is the acknowledgement that mistakes are a part of all our lives. They aren’t evidence of failure but evidence of how learning begins.

Counter-intuitively, kindness exists when we don’t try to ‘throw away’ their mistakes but keep them visible. Kindness accepts that mistakes are an integral part of who we are and that they are an integral part of our learning.
To accept the existence of mistakes as a part of how learning happens is to be kind. It’s also to be truly learning-focused.

I still think this is true but the poem made me realise that ‘yet’ is most useful when ‘getting better’ has already been experienced. If we haven’t got better at something, how do we know that the promise of ‘yet’ actually exists.
Our mistakes and their mistakes are a vital part of the proof of our getting better. Without a memory of our mistakes, getting better is almost impossible.
Rather than hiding the mistakes with a quick ‘yet’ as though that will make everything go away, it acknowledges the truth that we all know. Mistakes are embedded in learning.
